title: Spinosaurid tooth
localityBasis: Inferred from the sandstone in the pulp cavity and the auction description. To be confirmed against the invoice.
source: Artemis Gallery, lot 234 (a lot of ten spinosaurid teeth)
summary: A spinosaurid tooth crown with fluted enamel and a broken base. The micro-images show several features that are hard to fake, and the condition needs attention: enamel is lifting at a crack across the crown. Whether the tooth has been repaired is not yet established.

steps.name: Micro-imaging
steps.note: 17 stills and one 30-second video, Dino-Lite AM7115MZT.

steps.name: UV screening
steps.note: Filtered 365 nm light to reveal glue, filler or paint.

steps.name: Measurement and weight
steps.note: Calipers to 0.01 mm, scale to 0.01 g.

steps.name: Overall views with scale
steps.note: Six views of the whole tooth with a forensic scale.

steps.name: Condition report issued
steps.note: Sealed record, ready to share with a buyer or insurer.

confidence.claim: A genuine fossil, not a cast or replica
confidence.basis: Enamel crazing, a sand-filled pulp cavity and manganese dendrites.
Fluted enamel, its fine wrinkled texture and the shape of the base.

confidence.claim: From the Kem Kem Group, Morocco
confidence.basis: The sandstone infill matches. The invoice would make it stronger.
Spinosaurid species can't be told apart reliably from a single loose tooth.
Dated by the rock unit, not by testing the tooth.
Needs UV screening and a survey of the whole tooth.

natural: Fluted enamel with a fine wrinkled surface, typical of spinosaurid crowns.
A grid of drying cracks across the enamel, which is difficult to imitate.
Rounded, frosted sand grains cemented inside the pulp cavity, matching Kem Kem sandstone.
Branching black manganese dendrites on the dentine, which grow slowly in the ground.
Orange-brown iron staining and reddish sediment lodged in the low spots.
condition: Enamel is lifting beside the crack across the crown. This is the most urgent issue.
Patches of missing enamel expose the pale dentine.
The base is broken, and a crack runs across the crown.
Surface dust, mineral crust and fine white threads that may be fibers or mold.
open: Repair or restoration. The crack across the crown is where a glued break would sit.
Whether the tip is intact. It hasn't been imaged yet.

care: Brush off dust with a soft brush or an air blower. No water or solvents yet.
Keep it at 40–50% relative humidity, with silica gel and a hygrometer in the box.
Once fully documented, stabilize the lifting enamel with a reversible conservation adhesive such as Paraloid B-72.

plates.title: Fluted enamel
plates.text: Flutes run along the crown, with the fine wrinkled enamel texture typical of spinosaurids. The white specks are surface dust and mineral crust.

plates.title: Crack across the crown
plates.text: A crack crosses the crown with a small step in the enamel. A glued break would sit here if the tooth had been repaired. UV screening will tell.

plates.title: Lifting enamel
plates.text: A thin flake of enamel has lifted at the crack. Stabilize it once documentation is complete.

plates.title: Enamel loss, low magnification
plates.text: Flutes run the length of the crown. A patch of enamel is missing and the pale dentine shows through.

plates.title: Broken base, handheld
plates.text: A motion-blurred frame of the base, kept for completeness. Plate 6 shows the same view in focus.

plates.title: Broken base in section
plates.text: The pulp cavity is packed with sand, and black dendrites mark the dentine. Both point to long burial in sandstone.

plates.title: Dentine surface
plates.text: Dentine with orange iron staining. The fine white threads are probably fibers or mold. Brush gently and keep dry.

plates.title: Sand infill meets dentine
plates.text: Cemented sand grains in the pulp cavity, beside manganese-stained dentine.

plates.title: Quartz grains
plates.text: Rounded, frosted grains held by natural cement, consistent with the river sandstones of the Kem Kem Group.

plates.title: Manganese dendrites
plates.text: Branching manganese oxide growths. They form slowly in the ground and are rarely imitated convincingly.

plates.title: Iron staining near the base
plates.text: Orange-brown iron oxide staining with fine cracks through the dentine.

plates.title: Crazing beside a matrix patch
plates.text: Natural crackle in the enamel, next to a patch of reddish sediment still attached.

plates.title: Enamel edge over dentine
plates.text: The margin where enamel has broken away, over stained dentine.

plates.title: Enamel edge, second lighting
plates.text: The same margin under warmer light, showing how deep the staining runs.

plates.title: Crown base with sediment
plates.text: Dark enamel near the base, with sediment lodged in the low spots.

plates.title: Crown base, refocused
plates.text: The same view at a different focal plane.

plates.title: Enamel crazing
plates.text: A grid of fine drying cracks across the enamel surface.
